tool.name: PyTorch
tool.tagline: Pythonic deep learning with dynamic graphs, autograd and GPU tensors
tool.description: PyTorch is the most widely used deep learning framework in research and increasingly in production. It gives you GPU-accelerated tensors, automatic differentiation over ordinary Python code, and building blocks for neural networks, data loading and distributed training. Learning it lets you read and write most modern ML code, from small classifiers to large transformers.

concepts.name: Tensors: the core data type
concepts.summary: A tensor is an n-dimensional array with a dtype and a device, much like a NumPy array that can also live on a GPU.
concepts.why: Every input, weight, activation and gradient in PyTorch is a tensor, so everything else builds on it.
concepts.body:
A **tensor** (`torch.Tensor`) is a typed, n-dimensional array. If you know NumPy's `ndarray`, you already know most of it: tensors have a `shape`, a `dtype` and support element-wise math, slicing and broadcasting. Two things are new: a tensor has a **device** (`cpu`, `cuda`, `mps`) and it can record operations for automatic differentiation.

Create one from Python data with `torch.tensor(data)`. PyTorch infers the dtype: Python ints become `torch.int64`, floats become `torch.float32` (not float64 as in NumPy), and bools become `torch.bool`.

Useful attributes and methods:

- `t.shape` (or `t.size()`) returns a `torch.Size`, which behaves like a tuple.
- `t.ndim` is the number of dimensions, `t.numel()` the number of elements.
- `t.dtype` and `t.device` tell you how and where the data is stored.
- Indexing a single element still gives a 0-dimensional tensor; call `.item()` to get a plain Python number, and `.tolist()` for nested lists.

Tensors are the currency of the library: models take tensors in and return tensors out, and the training loop is a sequence of tensor operations. Getting comfortable printing shapes and dtypes is the most useful debugging habit you can build.
concepts.code:
import torch

t = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(t.shape)          # torch.Size([2, 3])
print(t.dtype)          # torch.int64
print(t.device)         # cpu
print(t.ndim, t.numel())  # 2 6

f = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
print(f.dtype)          # torch.float32

print(t[1, 2])          # tensor(6)
print(t[1, 2].item())   # 6
print(t.tolist())       # [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
takeaways: A tensor = n-d array + dtype + device (+ optional gradient tracking)
Python floats become float32 by default, unlike NumPy's float64
`.item()` turns a one-element tensor into a Python number
pitfalls: Comparing a 0-d tensor to a number and expecting a Python bool everywhere; use `.item()` when you need a plain value.

quiz.q: What is the dtype of torch.tensor([0.5, 1.5])?
quiz.explain: PyTorch's default floating dtype is float32; torch.double is the same as float64.

concepts.name: Creating tensors
concepts.summary: Build tensors with zeros, ones, arange, linspace, full, eye and the random factories, and seed them for repeatability.
concepts.why: Initialising weights, masks, ranges and test inputs all start with these factory functions.
concepts.body:
Besides `torch.tensor(data)`, PyTorch has **factory functions** that create tensors of a given shape directly. They mirror NumPy:

- `torch.zeros(2, 3)`, `torch.ones(...)`, `torch.full((2, 2), 7.0)` fill with a constant.
- `torch.arange(start, end, step)` gives evenly spaced integers (end excluded); `torch.linspace(a, b, n)` gives `n` floats including both ends.
- `torch.eye(n)` is the identity matrix.
- `torch.rand` (uniform in [0, 1)), `torch.randn` (standard normal) and `torch.randint(low, high, shape)` produce random values.

Every factory accepts keyword arguments `dtype=` and `device=`, so you can create a tensor directly where it is needed instead of creating it on the CPU and copying it.

The `*_like` variants (`torch.zeros_like(x)`, `torch.randn_like(x)`) copy the shape, dtype and device of an existing tensor, which keeps code device-agnostic.

Random numbers come from a global generator. Call `torch.manual_seed(0)` at the start of a script to make runs repeatable. For finer control you can create a `torch.Generator`, seed it, and pass `generator=g` to a random function.

Prefer factories over building big Python lists and converting them: they are faster and never go through Python objects.
concepts.code:
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)                      # repeatable random numbers

print(torch.zeros(2, 3).shape)            # torch.Size([2, 3])
print(torch.arange(0, 10, 3))             # tensor([0, 3, 6, 9])
print(torch.linspace(0, 1, 5))            # tensor([0.0000, 0.2500, 0.5000, 0.7500, 1.0000])
print(torch.full((2,), 7.0))              # tensor([7., 7.])
print(torch.eye(2))                       # tensor([[1., 0.], [0., 1.]])
print(torch.ones(2, dtype=torch.int32))   # tensor([1, 1], dtype=torch.int32)

x = torch.randn(3, 4)                     # standard normal samples
print(torch.zeros_like(x).shape)          # torch.Size([3, 4])
print(torch.randint(0, 10, (5,)).dtype)   # torch.int64
takeaways: Factories take a shape plus optional `dtype=` and `device=`
`*_like` copies shape, dtype and device from another tensor
`torch.manual_seed` makes random tensors repeatable
pitfalls: Forgetting that `arange` excludes the end value while `linspace` includes it.

quiz.q: You need random noise with the same shape, dtype and device as tensor x. What is the cleanest call?
quiz.explain: randn_like copies shape, dtype and device; torch.randn(x.shape) would default to float32 on the CPU.

concepts.name: Dtypes and devices
concepts.summary: Choose numeric precision with dtype, move tensors between CPU and GPU with .to(), and know the type-promotion rules.
concepts.why: Most beginner runtime errors are dtype or device mismatches, and precision choices drive speed and memory.
concepts.body:
Every tensor has a **dtype** and a **device**. Common dtypes:

- `torch.float32`: the default for weights and activations.
- `torch.float16` and `torch.bfloat16`: 2-byte floats used for fast mixed-precision training.
- `torch.int64` (`torch.long`): indices and class labels; `CrossEntropyLoss` expects labels in this type.
- `torch.bool`: masks.

Convert with `t.to(torch.float32)` or shortcuts like `t.float()`, `t.long()`. Mixed-dtype arithmetic follows **type promotion**: `int64 + 0.5` gives float32, and true division `/` on integers always returns a float.

The **device** says where the data lives. `t.to("cuda")` copies a tensor to the first NVIDIA GPU, `"mps"` targets Apple silicon, and `"cpu"` brings it back. `.to()` returns a new tensor; it does not modify the original (modules are the exception, they move in place).

Operations require all operands on the same device. Adding a CPU tensor to a CUDA tensor raises `RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device`. The usual pattern is to pick a device once at the top of a script and create or move everything there:

```python
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
```

Moving data between host and GPU is relatively slow, so avoid round trips inside loops, such as calling `.item()` or `.cpu()` on every step.
concepts.code:
import torch

x = torch.arange(4)                     # int64
y = x.to(torch.float32) / 2
print(y)                                # tensor([0.0000, 0.5000, 1.0000, 1.5000])
print((x / 2).dtype)                    # torch.float32 (true division)
print((x + 0.5).dtype)                  # torch.float32 (type promotion)

h = y.to(torch.bfloat16)
print(h.dtype, h.element_size())        # torch.bfloat16 2

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
z = y.to(device)                        # copy (y itself is unchanged)
print(z.device.type)                    # cuda or cpu
print(y.device)                         # cpu
takeaways: float32 for weights, int64 for labels and indices, bool for masks
`.to(device)` returns a copy; operands must share one device
Integer `/` gives floats; mixed dtypes are promoted
pitfalls: Passing float labels to `CrossEntropyLoss` for class indices, or int64 inputs to a `Linear` layer.
Calling `.item()` every iteration, which forces a GPU sync.

quiz.q: a is a CPU tensor and b is a CUDA tensor. What does a + b do?
options: Moves a to the GPU automatically
quiz.explain: PyTorch never moves data implicitly between devices (0-d CPU scalars aside); you must call .to() yourself.

quiz.q: What is (torch.tensor([3, 4]) / 2).dtype?
quiz.explain: True division always produces a floating result, using the default float dtype float32.

concepts.name: Indexing and reshaping
concepts.summary: Slice, mask, reshape, permute, squeeze and combine tensors to get data into the shape a layer expects.
concepts.why: Shape wrangling is a large share of real deep learning code, from batching images to splitting attention heads.
concepts.body:
Indexing works like NumPy: `m[0]`, `m[:, 1]`, `m[1:, ::2]`, boolean masks `m[m > 8]` and integer index tensors. Basic slices return **views** that share memory with the original; masks and index tensors return copies.

Reshaping changes how the same elements are grouped:

- `x.view(3, 4)` reinterprets memory without copying; it needs a compatible memory layout.
- `x.reshape(3, 4)` does the same but copies when it has to. One dimension may be `-1` to be inferred.
- `x.flatten()` gives 1-d; `nn.Flatten` in models keeps the batch dimension.
- `x.unsqueeze(0)` adds a size-1 dimension (e.g. a batch of one), `x.squeeze()` removes them.
- `x.permute(2, 0, 1)` reorders dimensions, e.g. images from H, W, C to C, H, W; `x.T` or `x.transpose(0, 1)` swaps two.

Combining: `torch.cat(tensors, dim)` joins along an existing dimension, `torch.stack(tensors, dim)` creates a new one.

Convention matters: PyTorch layers expect the **batch dimension first**, and images as `N, C, H, W`. After `permute` or `transpose`, the tensor is usually non-contiguous, so `view` fails with a stride error; use `reshape` or call `.contiguous()` first.
concepts.code:
import torch

x = torch.arange(12)
m = x.view(3, 4)
print(m[:, 1])                        # tensor([1, 5, 9])
print(m[m > 8])                       # tensor([ 9, 10, 11])
print(m.T.shape)                      # torch.Size([4, 3])
print(m.unsqueeze(0).shape)           # torch.Size([1, 3, 4])
print(m.reshape(-1, 6).shape)         # torch.Size([2, 6])

img = torch.zeros(32, 32, 3)          # H, W, C
print(img.permute(2, 0, 1).shape)     # torch.Size([3, 32, 32])

print(torch.cat([m, m]).shape)        # torch.Size([6, 4])
print(torch.stack([m, m]).shape)      # torch.Size([2, 3, 4])
takeaways: Layers expect batch-first shapes; images are N, C, H, W
`view` never copies; `reshape` copies only if needed
`cat` joins along an existing dim, `stack` adds a new one
pitfalls: Calling `.view()` after `permute`/`transpose` and getting a stride error; use `.reshape()`.

quiz.q: t has shape (8, 3, 32, 32). What is torch.stack([t, t], dim=0).shape?
quiz.explain: stack inserts a new dimension of size 2 at position 0; cat would give (16, 3, 32, 32).

concepts.name: Tensor math and broadcasting
concepts.summary: Element-wise ops, matrix multiplication with @, reductions along a dim, broadcasting and in-place ops with a trailing underscore.
concepts.why: Neural networks are compositions of exactly these operations, so reading model code means reading tensor math.
concepts.body:
Arithmetic operators work **element-wise**: `a + b`, `a * b`, `a ** 2`, plus functions like `torch.exp`, `torch.sqrt` and `torch.relu`. Shapes must match or be **broadcastable**, with the same rules as NumPy: align shapes from the right; each dimension must be equal or 1. A bias of shape `(n,)` therefore adds to every row of a `(batch, n)` matrix.

`a @ b` (or `torch.matmul`) is matrix multiplication. With 3-d or higher inputs it multiplies the last two dimensions and broadcasts over the leading ones, which is how batched attention is written.

**Reductions** such as `sum`, `mean`, `max`, `argmax`, `std` take a `dim` argument and remove that dimension; pass `keepdim=True` to keep it as size 1 so the result still broadcasts against the input. `t.max(dim=1)` returns both `values` and `indices`.

Methods ending in an underscore are **in-place**: `a.add_(1)`, `a.zero_()`, `a.clamp_(0, 1)`. They save memory but overwrite data that autograd may need, so avoid them on tensors involved in gradient computation unless you know it is safe.

Everything runs on whatever device the tensors live on, with the same code.
concepts.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
b = torch.tensor([10., 20.])

print(a + b)            # tensor([[11., 22.], [13., 24.]])  b broadcast to each row
print(a * a)            # tensor([[ 1.,  4.], [ 9., 16.]])  element-wise
print(a @ a)            # tensor([[ 7., 10.], [15., 22.]])  matrix product

print(a.sum())                          # tensor(10.)
print(a.sum(dim=0))                     # tensor([4., 6.])
print(a.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True).shape)  # torch.Size([2, 1])
values, idx = a.max(dim=1)
print(values, idx)                      # tensor([2., 4.]) tensor([1, 1])

a.add_(1)                               # in place
print(a)                                # tensor([[2., 3.], [4., 5.]])
takeaways: `*` is element-wise, `@` is matrix multiplication
Reductions take `dim`; `keepdim=True` keeps broadcasting easy
A trailing underscore means the op modifies the tensor in place
pitfalls: Using `*` when you meant a matrix product, which silently broadcasts instead of failing.

quiz.q: x has shape (32, 10). What is x.mean(dim=0).shape?
quiz.explain: Reducing over dim 0 removes the batch dimension and leaves one mean per column.

concepts.name: NumPy interop
concepts.summary: Convert between tensors and NumPy arrays, knowing when memory is shared and when it is copied.
concepts.why: Data usually arrives as NumPy arrays and results often go back to NumPy, pandas or matplotlib.
concepts.body:
PyTorch and NumPy convert cheaply in both directions:

- `torch.from_numpy(a)` wraps a NumPy array as a tensor **sharing the same memory**: change one and you change the other. The dtype is kept, so a default NumPy float array becomes `float64`.
- `torch.tensor(a)` and `torch.as_tensor(a, dtype=...)` with a different dtype **copy**.
- `t.numpy()` returns an array sharing memory with a CPU tensor.

Two restrictions apply to `.numpy()`. The tensor must be on the CPU, and it must not require gradients. The standard idiom for getting results out of a model is therefore:

```python
arr = out.detach().cpu().numpy()
```

`detach()` drops the autograd history, and `cpu()` copies from the GPU if needed (it is a no-op for CPU tensors).

Watch the dtype on the way in. Models use float32 weights, so feeding them float64 tensors raises `expected scalar type Float but found Double`. Convert with `.float()` or `torch.from_numpy(a.astype(np.float32))`. Integer labels should be int64.

For plotting single values or logging, prefer `.item()` or `.tolist()` over converting a whole array.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import torch

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
t = torch.from_numpy(a)          # shares memory, dtype float64
a[0] = 100
print(t)                         # tensor([100.,   2.,   3.], dtype=torch.float64)

c = torch.tensor(a)              # independent copy
a[1] = -1
print(c[1].item())               # 2.0

x = t.float()                    # float32 for use with model weights
print(x.dtype)                   # torch.float32

w = torch.ones(2, requires_grad=True)
print(w.detach().cpu().numpy())  # [1. 1.]
# w.numpy() would raise: Can't call numpy() on Tensor that requires grad
takeaways: `from_numpy` and `.numpy()` share memory; `torch.tensor` copies
Use `.detach().cpu().numpy()` to export model outputs
NumPy floats are float64: convert to float32 before feeding a model
pitfalls: Mutating a NumPy array after `from_numpy` and being surprised the tensor changed too.

quiz.q: Why does model_output.numpy() fail inside a training script on a GPU?
options: The tensor is on the GPU and may require grad
numpy() only works on integer tensors
quiz.explain: numpy() needs a CPU tensor that does not require grad, hence detach().cpu().numpy().

concepts.name: Autograd: automatic gradients
concepts.summary: Mark tensors with requires_grad, call backward() on a scalar loss, and read gradients from .grad.
concepts.why: Gradients are what training follows; autograd computes them for any Python code you write.
concepts.body:
**Autograd** is PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine. When a tensor has `requires_grad=True`, every operation on it is recorded in a graph of functions. Calling `.backward()` on a scalar result walks that graph backwards and stores d(result)/d(tensor) in each leaf tensor's `.grad`.

Key facts:

- Parameters of `nn` layers already have `requires_grad=True`; input data does not.
- `backward()` needs a scalar (like a loss). For a non-scalar output, reduce it first with `.sum()` or `.mean()`.
- Gradients **accumulate**: a second `backward()` adds to `.grad` rather than replacing it. That is why training loops call `optimizer.zero_grad()` every step.
- Each result tensor has a `grad_fn` naming the operation that created it, e.g. `AddBackward0`.
- By default the graph is freed after `backward()`; calling it twice on the same graph raises an error unless you pass `retain_graph=True`.

The graph is built dynamically as your Python runs, so loops, `if` statements and function calls all work naturally. This **define-by-run** design is what makes PyTorch easy to debug: you can print tensors and step through with a debugger at any point.
concepts.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x ** 2 + 2 * x          # y = 15
y.backward()
print(x.grad)               # tensor(8.)   dy/dx = 2x + 2
print(y.grad_fn)            # <AddBackward0 object at ...>

w = torch.tensor([1.0, -2.0], requires_grad=True)
c = torch.tensor([3.0, 4.0])
(w * c).sum().backward()
print(w.grad)               # tensor([3., 4.])

(w * c).sum().backward()    # a new graph, gradients add up
print(w.grad)               # tensor([6., 8.])

w.grad = None               # reset, like optimizer.zero_grad()
takeaways: Set `requires_grad=True` on leaves; call `.backward()` on a scalar
Gradients accumulate in `.grad` until you clear them
The graph is rebuilt on every forward pass (define-by-run)
pitfalls: Forgetting to zero gradients, so each step uses the sum of all previous gradients.

quiz.q: You call loss.backward() twice (recomputing loss each time) without zeroing. What is in w.grad?
quiz.explain: backward() accumulates into .grad, which is why optimizers provide zero_grad().

concepts.name: nn.Module: defining models
concepts.summary: Subclass nn.Module, create layers in __init__, describe the computation in forward, and call the model like a function.
concepts.why: nn.Module is how every PyTorch model, layer and loss is structured, from a two-layer MLP to an LLM.
concepts.body:
A model is a class that inherits from `torch.nn.Module`. You create sub-layers in `__init__` and assign them to attributes; you describe how input flows through them in `forward`.

Assigning a module or `nn.Parameter` to `self` **registers** it. That registration is what makes these work automatically:

- `model.parameters()` and `model.named_parameters()` iterate all trainable weights (pass them to the optimizer).
- `model.to(device)` moves every parameter and buffer.
- `model.state_dict()` collects weights for saving.
- `model.train()` / `model.eval()` switch the mode of every sub-module.

Always call `super().__init__()` first, and call the model as `model(x)`, not `model.forward(x)`, so that hooks run.

Layers held in a plain Python list are **not** registered; use `nn.ModuleList` or `nn.ModuleDict` instead. For a simple stack of layers, `nn.Sequential(layer1, layer2, ...)` saves writing a class at all, and its items can be indexed like a list.

Because `forward` is ordinary Python, you can use loops, conditionals and print statements inside it, which makes custom architectures straightforward to write and debug.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, n_hidden, n_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_in, n_hidden)    # registered automatically
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(n_hidden, n_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(torch.relu(self.fc1(x)))

model = MLP(4, 16, 3)
out = model(torch.randn(8, 4))                   # call the model, not .forward
print(out.shape)                                 # torch.Size([8, 3])
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))  # 131
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    print(name, tuple(p.shape))   # fc1.weight (16, 4), fc1.bias (16,), ...

seq = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 3))
print(seq(torch.randn(8, 4)).shape)              # torch.Size([8, 3])
takeaways: Create layers in `__init__`, compute in `forward`, call `model(x)`
Attribute assignment registers parameters; plain lists do not
`nn.Sequential` covers simple layer stacks
pitfalls: Storing layers in a Python list, so the optimizer never sees their parameters; use `nn.ModuleList`.
Forgetting `super().__init__()`, which fails as soon as you assign a layer.

quiz.q: A model keeps its blocks in self.blocks = [nn.Linear(8, 8) for _ in range(3)]. What goes wrong?
options: forward cannot loop over a list
The blocks' parameters are not registered, so they are not trained or moved
Linear layers cannot be stored in lists
quiz.explain: Only Module and Parameter attributes (or ModuleList/ModuleDict) are registered with the parent module.

concepts.name: Common layers and activations
concepts.summary: Linear, Conv2d, pooling, Embedding, normalization, Dropout and activations, and how their input and output shapes relate.
concepts.why: Picking layers and getting their shapes right is the everyday work of model building.
concepts.body:
`torch.nn` provides ready-made layers. The ones you meet constantly:

- `nn.Linear(in, out)`: `y = x W^T + b` on the last dimension, any leading batch dims.
- `nn.Conv2d(in_ch, out_ch, kernel_size, stride, padding)`: 2-d convolution over `N, C, H, W` input. `padding=1` with a 3x3 kernel keeps H and W.
- `nn.MaxPool2d(2)`: halves H and W.
- `nn.Embedding(num, dim)`: a lookup table turning int64 token ids into vectors.
- `nn.BatchNorm2d(ch)` and `nn.LayerNorm(dim)`: normalization; LayerNorm is the norm of transformers.
- `nn.Dropout(p)`: randomly zeroes activations during training only.
- Activations: `nn.ReLU`, `nn.GELU`, `nn.SiLU`, `nn.Tanh`, `nn.Sigmoid`, `nn.Softmax(dim)`.

Most layers also exist as functions in `torch.nn.functional` (usually imported as `F`): `F.relu(x)`, `F.gelu(x)`. Use the module form for layers with weights; the functional form is fine for stateless operations inside `forward`.

If you do not want to compute an input size by hand, `nn.LazyLinear(out)` infers `in_features` on the first call.

Print shapes after each layer when building a new model; a mismatch error such as `mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (8x512 and 256x10)` tells you exactly which dimension to fix.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.randn(2, 3, 28, 28)                       # N, C, H, W
conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
print(conv(x).shape)                                # torch.Size([2, 8, 28, 28])
print(nn.MaxPool2d(2)(conv(x)).shape)               # torch.Size([2, 8, 14, 14])

emb = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=1000, embedding_dim=16)
tokens = torch.tensor([[1, 5, 42]])                 # int64 ids
h = emb(tokens)
print(h.shape)                                      # torch.Size([1, 3, 16])
print(nn.LayerNorm(16)(h).shape)                    # torch.Size([1, 3, 16])

print(F.gelu(torch.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])))       # tensor([-0.1587,  0.0000,  0.8413])
takeaways: Linear acts on the last dim; Conv2d expects N, C, H, W
Embedding maps int64 ids to vectors
Use modules for layers with weights, `F.*` for stateless ops
pitfalls: Hard-coding a Linear input size after conv layers and getting it wrong; print the shape or use `nn.LazyLinear`.

quiz.q: What does nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1) output for an input of shape (4, 3, 64, 64)?
quiz.explain: Padding 1 with a 3x3 kernel and stride 1 keeps the spatial size; channels become 16.

concepts.name: Loss functions
concepts.summary: Use CrossEntropyLoss with raw logits and int64 class labels, BCEWithLogitsLoss for binary or multi-label targets, MSELoss for regression.
concepts.why: The loss defines what the model learns; picking the wrong one, or feeding it the wrong format, silently ruins training.
concepts.body:
A **loss function** turns predictions and targets into one scalar to minimise. The common ones:

- `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` for single-label classification. It takes **raw logits** of shape `(N, C)` and **class indices** of shape `(N,)` as int64. It applies log-softmax internally, so do not put a softmax at the end of your model. It also accepts class probabilities as targets and has `label_smoothing=`.
- `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss` for binary or multi-label problems: logits and float targets of the same shape. It fuses the sigmoid for numerical stability.
- `nn.MSELoss` and `nn.L1Loss` (or `nn.SmoothL1Loss`) for regression.

All losses average over the batch by default (`reduction="mean"`); use `"sum"` or `"none"` to get per-sample values, for example to apply your own weights. `CrossEntropyLoss` also has `weight=` for imbalanced classes and `ignore_index=` for padding tokens.

Every loss has a functional twin in `torch.nn.functional`: `F.cross_entropy(logits, y)` is the same as the module.

Sanity check: at initialisation, cross-entropy over C balanced classes should be close to ln(C), about 2.3 for 10 classes. A much larger starting loss hints at a bug in scaling or labels.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.5, -1.0],
                       [0.1, 0.2, 3.0]])     # raw scores, no softmax
targets = torch.tensor([0, 2])               # class indices, int64
print(nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, targets))  # tensor(0.1755)

per_sample = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(reduction="none")(logits, targets)
print(per_sample.shape)                      # torch.Size([2])

bce = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
print(bce(torch.tensor([0.0]), torch.tensor([1.0])))   # tensor(0.6931) = ln 2

mse = nn.MSELoss()
print(mse(torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0]), torch.tensor([1.5, 2.0])))  # tensor(0.1250)
takeaways: CrossEntropyLoss: logits in, int64 class indices as targets
BCEWithLogitsLoss for binary and multi-label, float targets
Initial cross-entropy should be about ln(number of classes)
pitfalls: Applying softmax before CrossEntropyLoss, which double-normalises and slows learning.

quiz.q: Your classifier ends with nn.Softmax and you train with nn.CrossEntropyLoss. What is the problem?
options: CrossEntropyLoss already applies log-softmax, so softmax is applied twice
CrossEntropyLoss needs probabilities, so this is correct
quiz.explain: CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits; an extra softmax squashes them and weakens gradients.

concepts.name: Optimizers
concepts.summary: Use torch.optim (SGD, Adam, AdamW) to update parameters from their gradients with zero_grad, backward, step.
concepts.why: The optimizer and learning rate decide whether and how fast training converges.
concepts.body:
An **optimizer** owns a list of parameters and updates them from their `.grad`. Create it once, before the loop:

```python
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)
```

Each step is the same three calls: `opt.zero_grad()` clears old gradients, `loss.backward()` computes new ones, `opt.step()` applies the update.

Which optimizer?

- `SGD(lr, momentum=0.9)`: simple and strong for vision models with a tuned schedule.
- `Adam`: adaptive per-parameter step sizes, forgiving defaults (`lr=1e-3`).
- `AdamW`: Adam with decoupled weight decay; the default for transformers and most modern work.

The **learning rate** is the most important hyperparameter. Too high and the loss explodes or oscillates; too low and training crawls.

Optimizers can hold several **parameter groups** with different settings, for example no weight decay on biases and norms, or a smaller learning rate for a pretrained backbone:

```python
opt = torch.optim.AdamW([
    {"params": backbone.parameters(), "lr": 1e-5},
    {"params": head.parameters()},
], lr=1e-3)
```

Adam-style optimizers keep state (running averages) per parameter, roughly twice the model's size in memory, and that state must be saved with checkpoints to resume training exactly.
concepts.code:
import torch

w = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD([w, b], lr=0.1)

x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, 50)
y = 2 * x + 1                       # the line we want to recover

for step in range(200):
    loss = ((w * x + b - y) ** 2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad()                 # 1. clear old gradients
    loss.backward()                 # 2. compute new ones
    opt.step()                      # 3. update w and b

print(round(w.item(), 3), round(b.item(), 3))   # 2.0 1.0
takeaways: Loop: `zero_grad()`, `backward()`, `step()`
AdamW is the common default; SGD with momentum for many vision tasks
Parameter groups give different hyperparameters to different parts
pitfalls: Creating the optimizer before replacing a layer (e.g. a new head), so the new parameters are never updated.

quiz.q: Which order of calls inside a training step is correct?
quiz.explain: Clear stale gradients, compute fresh ones, then apply them; zeroing between backward and step would erase them.

concepts.name: The training loop
concepts.summary: Put it together: iterate over batches, forward, loss, backward, step, then evaluate under torch.no_grad.
concepts.why: PyTorch has no built-in fit(); you write this loop yourself, and every training script is a variation of it.
concepts.body:
PyTorch leaves the training loop to you. Its standard shape:

1. `model.train()` to enable training behaviour (dropout, batch-norm statistics).
2. For each batch: compute predictions, compute the loss, `opt.zero_grad()`, `loss.backward()`, `opt.step()`.
3. Periodically `model.eval()` and measure on validation data inside `with torch.no_grad():`, which skips building the autograd graph and saves memory.

One pass over the training data is an **epoch**. Shuffle the data each epoch and use mini-batches (typically 32 to 512 samples), which give noisy but cheap gradient estimates.

Track the loss as a Python float with `loss.item()` for logging, but not on every step on a GPU, since each call synchronises.

Debugging tips that save hours:

- First try to **overfit a single small batch**. If the loss does not go to near zero, there is a bug.
- Check the initial loss is plausible (about ln C for C classes).
- Watch both training and validation metrics; a growing gap means overfitting.

Higher-level wrappers such as PyTorch Lightning or Hugging Face `Trainer` generate this loop for you, but they are much easier to use once you have written it by hand.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.randn(512, 2)
y = (X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] > 0).long()          # label: same-sign quadrants

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 2))
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(100):
    model.train()
    perm = torch.randperm(len(X))            # shuffle each epoch
    for i in range(0, len(X), 64):
        idx = perm[i:i + 64]
        loss = loss_fn(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    acc = (model(X).argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean()
print(f"train accuracy {acc:.2f}")            # typically above 0.95
takeaways: train() / batches / zero_grad-backward-step / eval() + no_grad
Overfit one batch first to prove the pipeline works
Log `loss.item()` sparingly on GPUs
pitfalls: Evaluating without `model.eval()`, so dropout and batch-norm behave as in training.

quiz.q: Why wrap validation in torch.no_grad()?
options: It avoids recording the autograd graph, saving memory and time
quiz.explain: no_grad only disables graph recording; switching dropout off is model.eval()'s job.

concepts.name: Dataset and DataLoader
concepts.summary: Wrap data in a Dataset with __len__ and __getitem__, then let DataLoader batch, shuffle and load it in parallel.
concepts.why: Real data does not fit in one tensor; DataLoader is how PyTorch streams it efficiently into training.
concepts.body:
`torch.utils.data` separates **what** a sample is from **how** samples are batched.

A map-style **Dataset** implements `__len__` and `__getitem__(i)`, returning one sample, often an `(input, label)` tuple. Load lazily in `__getitem__` (read an image file, tokenize a line) so the dataset itself stays small. For tensors already in memory, `TensorDataset(X, y)` is enough, and `random_split` makes train/validation splits.

A **DataLoader** wraps a dataset and yields batches:

- `batch_size` and `shuffle=True` (for training; keep validation unshuffled).
- `num_workers=4` loads batches in background processes so the GPU is not left waiting.
- `pin_memory=True` speeds up copies to CUDA; `persistent_workers=True` avoids restarting workers each epoch.
- `drop_last=True` discards a final short batch, useful when batch size must be constant.
- `collate_fn` controls how samples are combined, for example padding variable-length sequences.

The default collate stacks tensors, numbers and NumPy arrays and preserves tuples and dicts, so `for xb, yb in loader:` just works.

With `num_workers > 0` on Windows and macOS, workers are started with spawn, so the script must keep its training code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`. For data that cannot be indexed, such as a stream, subclass `IterableDataset` instead.
takeaways: Dataset = how to get sample i; DataLoader = batching, shuffling, workers
Use `num_workers` and `pin_memory` to keep the GPU fed
`collate_fn` customises batching, e.g. padding
pitfalls: Doing expensive loading in `__init__` for huge datasets instead of lazily in `__getitem__`.

quiz.q: A DataLoader over 10 samples with batch_size=4 and drop_last=True yields how many batches?
quiz.explain: Two full batches of 4; the last 2 samples are dropped.

concepts.name: Training on a GPU
concepts.summary: Move the model and each batch to the accelerator, write device-agnostic code, and avoid hidden synchronisations.
concepts.why: GPUs make deep learning 10-100x faster, but only if data and model actually live there.
concepts.body:
To train on a GPU, put **both** the model and the data on it:

- `model.to(device)` moves all parameters and buffers in place. Do this before creating the optimizer.
- Each batch: `xb = xb.to(device, non_blocking=True)`. With `pin_memory=True` in the DataLoader, the copy can overlap with computation.

Write the device choice once and keep the rest device-agnostic. CUDA covers NVIDIA (and AMD via ROCm builds, which also use the `"cuda"` name); `"mps"` covers Apple silicon. Recent releases also offer `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()`, which picks whichever accelerator is present.

GPU work is **asynchronous**: Python queues kernels and continues. The CPU only waits when it needs a result, for example `.item()`, `.cpu()`, `print(tensor)` or an `if` on a tensor's value. Each of these is a **synchronisation**; too many in the inner loop starve the GPU. When timing GPU code, call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before reading the clock.

Check memory with `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` and `nvidia-smi`. If you run out of memory, reduce the batch size first, then look at mixed precision and gradient accumulation.

Common hiccups: tensors created inside `forward` with `torch.zeros(...)` land on the CPU; create them with `device=x.device` or `torch.zeros_like`.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available()
    else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available()
    else "cpu")

model = nn.Linear(10, 2).to(device)               # move parameters first
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

x = torch.randn(64, 10).to(device, non_blocking=True)
mask = torch.ones(64, 1, device=x.device)          # create new tensors on the same device

loss = (model(x) * mask).pow(2).mean()
opt.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
opt.step()
print(loss.device.type, round(loss.item(), 3))     # .item() synchronises and copies to CPU

if device.type == "cuda":
    torch.cuda.synchronize()                       # before timing anything
    print(torch.cuda.memory_allocated() // 2**20, "MiB allocated")
takeaways: Model and data must both be on the device
GPU calls are async; `.item()`, `.cpu()` and printing synchronise
Create tensors inside `forward` with `device=x.device`
pitfalls: Moving the inputs to the GPU but forgetting the targets, which fails inside the loss.

quiz.q: Why can timing a CUDA forward pass with time.time() before and after give a misleadingly small number?
options: CUDA kernels run asynchronously, so the call returns before the work finishes
The GPU clock differs from the CPU clock
quiz.explain: Without torch.cuda.synchronize() you only measure how long it took to queue the kernels.

concepts.name: train/eval modes and no_grad
concepts.summary: Know what model.eval() changes, when to use torch.no_grad or torch.inference_mode, and what detach() does.
concepts.why: Mixing these up gives wrong validation numbers, random predictions or out-of-memory errors at inference.
concepts.body:
Two independent switches control inference, and you usually want both.

**`model.train()` / `model.eval()`** set a flag on every sub-module. Only some layers react: `Dropout` stops dropping, and `BatchNorm` uses its running statistics instead of the batch's. Forgetting `eval()` makes predictions random (dropout) or batch-dependent (batch norm).

**`torch.no_grad()`** is a context manager (also a decorator) that stops autograd from recording operations. Outputs have `requires_grad=False`, no graph is kept and memory use drops. **`torch.inference_mode()`** is a stricter, slightly faster version: tensors created inside cannot be used in autograd later. Use it for pure inference and serving.

**`t.detach()`** returns a tensor sharing data with `t` but cut off from the graph. Use it when you want a value without its history: logging, storing outputs across steps, or feeding a target network.

A typical evaluation helper:

```python
@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, loader):
    model.eval()
    ...
```

Remember to switch back with `model.train()` before the next training epoch, since `eval()` persists until changed.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(100, 100), nn.Dropout(p=0.5))
x = torch.ones(1, 100)

model.train()
print(torch.equal(model(x), model(x)))   # False: different dropout masks
model.eval()
print(torch.equal(model(x), model(x)))   # True: dropout disabled

with torch.no_grad():
    y = model(x)
print(y.requires_grad)                   # False

with torch.inference_mode():
    z = model(x)
print(z.is_inference())                  # True

w = model[0].weight * 2
print(w.requires_grad, w.detach().requires_grad)   # True False
takeaways: `eval()` changes layer behaviour; `no_grad()` stops graph recording
Use both for validation and inference
`detach()` keeps the values but drops the history
pitfalls: Accumulating `total_loss += loss` across steps, which keeps every graph alive; use `loss.item()` or `loss.detach()`.

quiz.q: Inside torch.no_grad(), a model with Dropout is still in train mode. What happens?
quiz.explain: no_grad only affects autograd; layer behaviour depends on train()/eval().

concepts.name: Saving and loading checkpoints
concepts.summary: Save state_dicts of the model and optimizer with torch.save, and load them safely with torch.load(weights_only=True).
concepts.why: Long training runs crash and models must be shipped; checkpoints make both possible.
concepts.body:
The recommended way to persist a model is its **state_dict**: an ordered dict mapping parameter and buffer names to tensors. Save it rather than the whole model object, because pickling the object ties the file to your exact class and module layout.

To resume training you need more than weights: save a **checkpoint dict** with the model, optimizer (Adam's moment estimates), scheduler, epoch and anything else you track.

Loading:

- Rebuild the model with the same code, then `model.load_state_dict(sd)`. It reports missing or unexpected keys; `strict=False` tolerates them, for example when loading a backbone into a model with a new head.
- `torch.load(path, map_location="cpu")` loads GPU-saved tensors on a CPU-only machine.
- Since PyTorch 2.6, `torch.load` defaults to `weights_only=True`, which only unpickles tensors and basic containers. That protects you from malicious pickle files; keep it on and avoid saving arbitrary objects.

Call `model.eval()` after loading for inference. Models wrapped by `torch.compile` or `DistributedDataParallel` prefix their keys (`_orig_mod.`, `module.`), so save the underlying module's state_dict.

For sharing models outside Python, look at `torch.export` or the safetensors format used by the Hugging Face ecosystem.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Linear(3, 1)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters())
print(list(model.state_dict().keys()))     # ['weight', 'bias']

torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(),
            "opt": opt.state_dict(),
            "epoch": 5}, "ckpt.pt")

ckpt = torch.load("ckpt.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
model2 = nn.Linear(3, 1)                   # rebuild the architecture in code
model2.load_state_dict(ckpt["model"])
opt2 = torch.optim.Adam(model2.parameters())
opt2.load_state_dict(ckpt["opt"])

print(ckpt["epoch"])                       # 5
print(torch.equal(model.weight, model2.weight))   # True
takeaways: Save `state_dict()`s, not whole model objects
A resumable checkpoint includes optimizer state and the epoch
`torch.load` uses `weights_only=True` by default; use `map_location` across devices
pitfalls: Saving only the model weights and then resuming with a fresh Adam optimizer, which causes a loss spike.

quiz.q: Why is saving model.state_dict() preferred over torch.save(model)?
options: It produces a smaller file format
It avoids pickling your class, so the file survives code refactors and loads safely
quiz.explain: A state_dict is just named tensors; the whole-model pickle depends on your exact class definitions and needs unsafe unpickling.

concepts.name: Convolutional networks
concepts.summary: Build an image classifier from conv, activation and pooling blocks, compute feature-map sizes, and use torchvision.
concepts.why: CNNs remain the workhorse for vision tasks on modest compute, and they teach how architectures are composed.
concepts.body:
A **convolutional network** stacks blocks of `Conv2d -> (BatchNorm2d) -> ReLU -> pooling`. Early layers detect edges and textures, later ones larger patterns, while pooling shrinks the spatial size and the channel count grows. A small head (flatten or global pooling, then `Linear`) produces class logits.

The output size of a conv or pool along one spatial dimension is:

`floor((H + 2*padding - kernel) / stride) + 1`

so 3x3 kernels with `padding=1` keep the size, and `MaxPool2d(2)` halves it. Instead of computing the flattened size by hand, end with `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)` (global average pooling), which works for any input resolution, or use `nn.LazyLinear`.

The **torchvision** package supplies datasets (`MNIST`, `CIFAR10`, `ImageFolder`), image transforms and pretrained models. Its `torchvision.transforms.v2` API converts images to tensors, normalises them and applies augmentation such as random crops and flips, which is the cheapest way to reduce overfitting.

Use `BatchNorm2d` after convolutions in deeper nets (then set `bias=False` on the conv), and remember that training images need augmentation but validation images only need resizing and normalising.
takeaways: Conv-ReLU-pool blocks shrink space and grow channels
Size = floor((H + 2p - k) / s) + 1
Global average pooling or LazyLinear avoid hand-computed sizes
pitfalls: Applying training augmentations to the validation set, which makes metrics noisy and pessimistic.

quiz.q: A 32x32 input passes through Conv2d(k=3, padding=1), MaxPool2d(2), Conv2d(k=3, padding=1), MaxPool2d(2). What is the spatial size?
quiz.explain: The padded convs keep the size; each pool halves it: 32 -> 16 -> 8.

concepts.name: Embeddings and recurrent layers
concepts.summary: Turn token ids into vectors, pad batches of sequences, and run LSTMs with batch_first and packed sequences.
concepts.why: Text, time series and event data are sequences; these are the building blocks before (and inside) transformers.
concepts.body:
Sequence models start with an **embedding**: `nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim)` maps each int64 token id to a learned vector, so a batch of shape `(N, T)` becomes `(N, T, dim)`. Set `padding_idx=0` so the padding token's vector stays zero and gets no gradient.

Batches need equal lengths, so shorter sequences are **padded** (`nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence` does this in a `collate_fn`).

Recurrent layers `nn.RNN`, `nn.GRU` and `nn.LSTM` process the sequence step by step. Pass `batch_first=True` to use `(N, T, features)` like the rest of your code. An LSTM returns `output` (the hidden state at every step) and a tuple `(h_n, c_n)` holding the final states with shape `(num_layers * directions, N, hidden)`.

With padding, the "final" state would include pad steps. **Packing** fixes that: `pack_padded_sequence(x, lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)` lets the RNN skip pads, so `h_n` is the state after each sequence's last real token.

For new NLP work, transformers have largely replaced RNNs, but embeddings, padding and masks carry over directly, and GRUs and LSTMs remain useful for small streaming and time-series models.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

emb = nn.Embedding(100, 8, padding_idx=0)
lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=8, hidden_size=16, batch_first=True)

tokens = torch.tensor([[5, 7, 9, 0],
                       [3, 4, 0, 0]])          # padded with 0
out, (h, c) = lstm(emb(tokens))
print(out.shape)        # torch.Size([2, 4, 16])  every time step
print(h.shape)          # torch.Size([1, 2, 16])  (layers, batch, hidden)

lengths = torch.tensor([3, 2])
packed = nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence(
    emb(tokens), lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)
_, (h, _) = lstm(packed)
print(h[-1].shape)      # torch.Size([2, 16])  state after the last real token
takeaways: Embedding: (N, T) int64 ids -> (N, T, dim)
Use `batch_first=True`; h_n is (layers*dirs, N, hidden)
Pack padded batches so final states ignore padding
pitfalls: Taking `output[:, -1]` as the sequence summary when sequences are right-padded; it is often a pad step.

quiz.q: Why set padding_idx=0 in nn.Embedding?
options: Token 0's vector stays fixed at zero and receives no gradient
It makes token 0 the start-of-sequence token
It removes token 0 from the vocabulary
quiz.explain: padding_idx keeps the pad embedding at zero and excludes it from gradient updates.

concepts.name: Learning-rate schedules
concepts.summary: Change the learning rate during training with torch.optim.lr_scheduler: step decay, cosine, warmup and OneCycle.
concepts.why: A good schedule (often warmup plus cosine decay) gives better final accuracy than any fixed learning rate.
concepts.body:
A **learning-rate scheduler** wraps an optimizer and adjusts each param group's `lr` when you call `scheduler.step()`. Call it **after** `optimizer.step()`, either once per epoch or once per batch, depending on how the scheduler was configured.

Common choices in `torch.optim.lr_scheduler`:

- `StepLR(opt, step_size, gamma)`: multiply by `gamma` every `step_size` steps.
- `CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max)`: smooth decay along a cosine curve to near zero.
- `OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr, total_steps)`: warm up then anneal, stepped every batch; popular for fast training.
- `LinearLR` for warmup, combined with another schedule via `SequentialLR`.
- `ReduceLROnPlateau(opt)`: lower the rate when a monitored metric stops improving; call `scheduler.step(val_loss)`.

Transformers are almost always trained with a short **linear warmup** (a few hundred to a few thousand steps) followed by cosine or linear decay. Warmup avoids unstable early updates while Adam's statistics are still poor.

```python
warm = LinearLR(opt, start_factor=0.1, total_iters=500)
cos = CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=9500)
sched = SequentialLR(opt, [warm, cos], milestones=[500])
```

`scheduler.get_last_lr()` returns the current rates for logging, and schedulers have a `state_dict()` to save in checkpoints.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Linear(2, 1)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(opt, step_size=2, gamma=0.5)

for epoch in range(6):
    # ... one epoch of training, calling opt.step() per batch ...
    opt.step()
    print(epoch, sched.get_last_lr())
    sched.step()                 # after the optimizer step
# 0 [0.1]
# 1 [0.1]
# 2 [0.05]
# 3 [0.05]
# 4 [0.025]
# 5 [0.025]
takeaways: Call `scheduler.step()` after `optimizer.step()`
Warmup plus cosine decay is the modern default
Save the scheduler's state_dict with checkpoints
pitfalls: Stepping a per-batch scheduler (like OneCycleLR) only once per epoch, so the schedule barely moves.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of learning-rate warmup?
options: To reach a higher final accuracy by ending with a large rate
To avoid unstable updates at the start, when gradients and optimizer statistics are unreliable
quiz.explain: Starting small lets Adam's moment estimates settle before large steps are taken.

concepts.name: Gradient clipping and accumulation
concepts.summary: Cap the gradient norm to stabilise training, and accumulate gradients over micro-batches to simulate a bigger batch.
concepts.why: Both are standard in large-model training: clipping prevents loss spikes, accumulation fits big effective batches in small memory.
concepts.body:
**Gradient clipping** rescales gradients when their combined norm exceeds a threshold:

```python
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
```

Call it after `backward()` and before `step()`. It returns the total norm before clipping, which is worth logging: sudden spikes signal instability. Clipping is routine for transformers and RNNs, where occasional huge gradients would otherwise wreck the weights.

**Gradient accumulation** uses the fact that gradients add up across `backward()` calls. Run several micro-batches, calling `backward()` on each, and only then `step()` and `zero_grad()`. With 4 micro-batches of 8, the update matches one batch of 32, at the memory cost of 8.

Two details make it correct:

- Divide each micro-batch loss by the number of accumulation steps, so the summed gradient equals the gradient of the mean loss.
- Count learning-rate scheduler steps per optimizer step, not per micro-batch.

Layers that use batch statistics, like BatchNorm, still only see the micro-batch, so accumulation is not perfectly equivalent for them. Under DistributedDataParallel, wrap the non-final micro-batches in `model.no_sync()` to skip redundant gradient communication.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Linear(10, 1)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
accum = 4                                         # effective batch = 4 * 8
data = [(torch.randn(8, 10), torch.randn(8, 1)) for _ in range(8)]

opt.zero_grad()
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(data):
    loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(xb), yb) / accum
    loss.backward()                               # gradients add up
    if (i + 1) % accum == 0:
        norm = nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad()
        print(f"update after batch {i}, norm before clipping {norm:.2f}")
# prints two updates: after batch 3 and batch 7
takeaways: Clip after `backward()`, before `step()`; log the returned norm
Accumulate: scale loss by 1/steps, step every N micro-batches
Scheduler steps count optimizer updates, not micro-batches
pitfalls: Forgetting to divide the loss by the accumulation steps, which multiplies the effective learning rate.

quiz.q: You accumulate gradients over 4 micro-batches without dividing the loss by 4. The effect is roughly that...
options: the gradient, and so the effective learning rate, is 4x larger
only the last micro-batch is used
quiz.explain: Summed gradients of four mean losses are four times the gradient of the overall mean loss.

concepts.name: Transfer learning and fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Start from pretrained torchvision weights, freeze the backbone, replace the head, then optionally fine-tune with a small learning rate.
concepts.why: With pretrained models, a few hundred labelled images can give results that would otherwise need millions.
concepts.body:
**Transfer learning** reuses a network trained on a large dataset (such as ImageNet) as a feature extractor for your task. torchvision makes it a few lines:

```python
weights = ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT
model = resnet18(weights=weights)
preprocess = weights.transforms()
```

The `weights` object also provides the exact preprocessing (resize, crop, normalisation) the model was trained with; using different preprocessing quietly hurts accuracy.

The standard recipe:

1. **Freeze** the pretrained parameters with `p.requires_grad_(False)`.
2. **Replace the head**: the final layer (`model.fc` for ResNets, `model.classifier` for many others) with a new `nn.Linear` sized for your classes. New layers are trainable by default.
3. Train only the head, passing just the trainable parameters to the optimizer.
4. Optionally **fine-tune**: unfreeze some or all layers and continue with a learning rate 10-100x smaller, often via parameter groups.

Frozen BatchNorm layers still update their running statistics in `train()` mode; for very small datasets, keep the backbone in `eval()` mode.

The same pattern applies to text and audio models from the Hugging Face hub, which are PyTorch `nn.Module`s under the hood.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torchvision.models import resnet18, ResNet18_Weights

weights = ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT
model = resnet18(weights=weights)           # downloads ImageNet weights once
preprocess = weights.transforms()           # matching resize + normalise

for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad_(False)                 # freeze the backbone

model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, 5)   # new 5-class head, trainable

trainable = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
print(sum(p.numel() for p in trainable))    # 2565  (512 * 5 + 5)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(trainable, lr=1e-3)

x = preprocess(torch.rand(3, 300, 400)).unsqueeze(0)   # fake image
print(model(x).shape)                       # torch.Size([1, 5])
takeaways: Use the weights' own `transforms()` for preprocessing
Freeze, replace the head, train the head, then fine-tune gently
Give the optimizer only trainable parameters
pitfalls: Fine-tuning the whole network with a large learning rate, destroying the pretrained features.

quiz.q: After freezing a ResNet and assigning model.fc = nn.Linear(512, 5), which parameters are trainable?
options: None, since the model was frozen
quiz.explain: The freeze happened before the new layer existed, and new layers default to requires_grad=True.

concepts.name: Reproducibility and seeding
concepts.summary: Seed every random source, control DataLoader randomness, and opt into deterministic algorithms when you need identical runs.
concepts.why: Comparing experiments and debugging require runs you can repeat.
concepts.body:
Randomness enters training through weight initialisation, data shuffling, augmentation, dropout and some GPU kernels. To repeat a run:

- Seed all generators: Python's `random`, NumPy and PyTorch. `torch.manual_seed` seeds the CPU and all CUDA devices.
- Give the DataLoader its own seeded `torch.Generator` via `generator=`. Each worker process derives its PyTorch seed from it; seed NumPy and `random` inside workers with a `worker_init_fn` if your dataset uses them.
- Call `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` to make PyTorch raise an error whenever an operation has no deterministic implementation, and set `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False` so cuDNN does not pick kernels by timing. Some CUDA matmul paths also need the environment variable `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8`.

Deterministic mode can be slower, so many teams only enable it when debugging.

Even with all of this, results are only guaranteed identical on the same hardware, driver and PyTorch version. Different GPUs, batch sizes or numbers of workers change floating-point summation order. For research claims, report the mean and spread over several seeds rather than chasing bit-exact runs.
concepts.code:
import random
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

def seed_everything(seed: int) -> None:
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)         # CPU and all CUDA devices

seed_everything(42)
a = torch.randn(3)
seed_everything(42)
b = torch.randn(3)
print(torch.equal(a, b))            # True

g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
loader = DataLoader(list(range(10)), batch_size=5, shuffle=True, generator=g)
print([batch.tolist() for batch in loader])   # same order on every run

torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)      # error on nondeterministic ops
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
takeaways: Seed `random`, NumPy and torch; give DataLoaders a seeded generator
`use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` surfaces nondeterministic ops
Bit-exactness holds only on identical hardware and versions
pitfalls: Seeding only torch while the dataset's augmentation uses NumPy's global RNG.

quiz.q: What does torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) do when an op has no deterministic implementation?
options: Silently falls back to the CPU
quiz.explain: It makes nondeterminism explicit by raising, so you can find and replace the offending op.

concepts.name: Automatic mixed precision
concepts.summary: Run matmuls in bfloat16 or float16 with torch.autocast, scale fp16 losses with GradScaler, and enable TF32.
concepts.why: Mixed precision typically gives 2-3x faster training and halves activation memory on modern GPUs.
concepts.body:
**Mixed precision** keeps weights in float32 but runs most computation in a 16-bit type. Tensor cores on modern GPUs are much faster in 16-bit, and activations take half the memory.

`torch.autocast(device_type, dtype)` is a context manager around the **forward pass and loss**. Inside it, ops that benefit (matmul, convolutions) run in low precision, while numerically sensitive ones (softmax, losses, reductions) are kept in float32 automatically. Run `backward()` outside the context.

Pick the dtype:

- **bfloat16** has float32's exponent range, so it rarely underflows. It is the default choice on Ampere-or-newer GPUs and TPUs, and needs no extra machinery.
- **float16** has more mantissa but a narrow range; small gradients underflow to zero. Use `torch.amp.GradScaler`, which multiplies the loss by a large factor before `backward()`, unscales before the step, and skips steps that produced inf or NaN.

If you clip gradients with a scaler, call `scaler.unscale_(opt)` before clipping.

Separately, `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")` lets float32 matmuls use **TF32** tensor cores on NVIDIA GPUs, a near-free speedup for code you do not convert.

Keep the model's weights in float32 (do not call `model.half()` for training); autocast handles the casts.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.bfloat16
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 10)).to(device)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(device, enabled=(dtype == torch.float16))

x = torch.randn(64, 512, device=device)
y = torch.randint(0, 10, (64,), device=device)

with torch.autocast(device_type=device, dtype=dtype):
    logits = model(x)                          # matmuls in 16-bit
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits, y)
print(logits.dtype, loss.dtype)                # 16-bit logits, float32 loss

scaler.scale(loss).backward()                  # backward outside autocast
scaler.step(opt)                               # unscales; skips inf/NaN steps
scaler.update()
opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
takeaways: autocast wraps forward + loss; backward goes outside
bfloat16 needs no scaler; float16 needs GradScaler
Keep master weights in float32
pitfalls: Clipping gradients that are still scaled; call `scaler.unscale_(opt)` first.

quiz.q: Why does float16 training need a GradScaler but bfloat16 usually does not?
options: float16's small exponent range makes tiny gradients underflow to zero
bfloat16 is computed in float32 internally
quiz.explain: bfloat16 shares float32's exponent range, so small gradients survive without loss scaling.

concepts.name: torch.compile
concepts.summary: Speed up models with one line: torch.compile captures Python into graphs and generates fused kernels, with caveats about graph breaks and recompiles.
concepts.why: torch.compile often gives 1.3-2x speedups on training and inference with no model rewrite.
concepts.body:
`torch.compile(model)` returns an optimised wrapper around a module or function. It works in layers:

- **TorchDynamo** hooks into Python bytecode execution and captures tensor operations into an FX graph, guarded by checks on shapes, dtypes and Python values.
- **AOTAutograd** traces the backward pass ahead of time.
- **TorchInductor** (the default backend) generates fused kernels: Triton on GPUs, C++/OpenMP on CPUs.

The first call is slow because it compiles; later calls reuse the cached code while the guards still hold.

Things to know:

- **Graph breaks**: code Dynamo cannot trace (some third-party calls, data-dependent Python control flow, `print` of tensor values) splits the graph and falls back to Python, costing performance. `fullgraph=True` turns breaks into errors so you can find them.
- **Recompilation**: a change in a guarded property, such as a new input shape, triggers a recompile. After a shape changes, Dynamo marks that dimension dynamic; you can also pass `dynamic=True` or call `torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic`.
- **Modes**: `"reduce-overhead"` uses CUDA graphs for small batches, `"max-autotune"` benchmarks kernel variants (slow compile, fastest run).

Debug with `TORCH_LOGS="graph_breaks,recompiles"`. The compiled module shares parameters with the original, so the optimizer and state_dict work as before (keys gain an `_orig_mod.` prefix).
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))
compiled = torch.compile(model)          # same parameters, optimised execution

x = torch.randn(32, 256)
out = compiled(x)                        # first call: trace + compile (slow)
out = compiled(x)                        # later calls: cached kernels
print(torch.allclose(out, model(x), atol=1e-5))   # True

@torch.compile(fullgraph=True)           # error instead of a silent graph break
def scaled_gelu(x, s):
    return nn.functional.gelu(x) * s

print(scaled_gelu(torch.randn(4), 2.0).shape)     # torch.Size([4])

# Find graph breaks and recompiles from the shell:
#   TORCH_LOGS="graph_breaks,recompiles" python train.py
takeaways: Dynamo captures graphs, Inductor generates fused kernels
First call compiles; guards decide when to recompile
Use `fullgraph=True` and TORCH_LOGS to hunt graph breaks
pitfalls: Benchmarking the first call, which includes compilation time.
Feeding constantly changing shapes, causing repeated recompiles.

quiz.q: What is a graph break in torch.compile?
options: A crash in the compiled code
A point where Dynamo cannot trace, so the graph is split and Python runs in between
quiz.explain: Graph breaks keep the program correct but reduce how much can be fused and optimised.

concepts.name: Custom autograd Functions
concepts.summary: Define your own forward and backward with torch.autograd.Function, save tensors on ctx, and verify with gradcheck.
concepts.why: Needed for straight-through estimators, numerically stable gradients, and wrapping non-PyTorch code.
concepts.body:
When autograd's automatic derivative is not what you want, subclass `torch.autograd.Function` and write both directions yourself:

- `forward(ctx, *inputs)`: compute the output. Store what backward needs with `ctx.save_for_backward(*tensors)`; non-tensor values can be set as attributes on `ctx`.
- `backward(ctx, *grad_outputs)`: receive the gradient of the loss with respect to each output and return one gradient per forward input, or `None` for inputs that need none (like integer arguments).

Both methods are `@staticmethod`s, and you call the function with `MyFn.apply(x)`, never by instantiating it. Recent PyTorch versions also support splitting out a `setup_context(ctx, inputs, output)` method, which is required for compatibility with `torch.func` transforms.

Typical uses:

- **Straight-through estimators**: round or binarise in the forward pass but pretend it was identity in the backward pass, as in quantisation-aware training.
- **Stable or cheaper gradients** for a fused formula.
- Wrapping code autograd cannot see, such as a NumPy or C++ routine.

Always check a hand-written backward with `torch.autograd.gradcheck`, which compares it to finite differences. Use float64 inputs, because float32 is too imprecise for the check.
takeaways: Static `forward`/`backward`; call with `Fn.apply(...)`
Return one gradient per input, `None` where not needed
Verify with `gradcheck` on float64
pitfalls: Returning fewer gradients from backward than forward had inputs, which raises an error.

quiz.q: forward(ctx, x, k) takes a tensor x and a Python int k. What should backward return?
options: grad_x and a gradient for k as a tensor
quiz.explain: backward returns one value per forward input in order; non-differentiable inputs get None.

concepts.name: Forward and backward hooks
concepts.summary: Attach functions to modules and tensors to inspect or modify activations and gradients without changing model code.
concepts.why: Hooks power feature extraction, activation statistics, gradient debugging and interpretability tools.
concepts.body:
A **hook** is a callback PyTorch runs at a specific point. Registering one returns a handle; call `handle.remove()` when done, or the hook keeps running (and keeps references alive).

- `module.register_forward_hook(fn)` calls `fn(module, inputs, output)` after `forward`. Returning a value replaces the output. Use it to capture intermediate activations.
- `module.register_forward_pre_hook(fn)` runs before `forward` and can modify inputs.
- `module.register_full_backward_hook(fn)` calls `fn(module, grad_input, grad_output)` during backward.
- `tensor.register_hook(fn)` calls `fn(grad)` when that tensor's gradient is computed; returning a tensor replaces the gradient. Handy for gradient clipping on one tensor or for inspecting non-leaf gradients.

Typical uses:

- Extract embeddings from a pretrained network's penultimate layer.
- Log activation means and standard deviations per layer to diagnose dead ReLUs or exploding values.
- Build saliency and Grad-CAM style visualisations from activations plus gradients.

Store `output.detach()` in forward hooks unless you need gradients through it; otherwise you keep the graph alive. Hooks only fire when the module is called via `module(x)`, not `module.forward(x)`. For torchvision models, `torchvision.models.feature_extraction.create_feature_extractor` is a cleaner alternative for pulling out named layers.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 8), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(8, 2))
acts = {}

def save_output(name):
    def hook(module, inputs, output):
        acts[name] = output.detach()
    return hook

handle = model[1].register_forward_hook(save_output("relu"))
model(torch.randn(3, 4))
print(acts["relu"].shape)                     # torch.Size([3, 8])
print((acts["relu"] == 0).float().mean())     # fraction of dead units in this batch
handle.remove()                               # stop capturing

x = torch.randn(3, 4, requires_grad=True)
x.register_hook(lambda g: print("input grad shape", g.shape))
model(x).sum().backward()                     # input grad shape torch.Size([3, 4])
takeaways: Forward hooks see (module, inputs, output); returning a value replaces output
`tensor.register_hook` sees and can rewrite gradients
Keep the handle and `remove()` it
pitfalls: Saving `output` without `.detach()`, which keeps the whole autograd graph in memory.

quiz.q: What does a forward hook's return value do if it is not None?
options: It is added to the loss
quiz.explain: Forward hooks may return a modified output; forward pre-hooks may return modified inputs.

concepts.name: Profiling and benchmarking
concepts.summary: Find where time goes with torch.profiler, label regions with record_function, and benchmark correctly with torch.utils.benchmark.
concepts.why: Optimising without measuring wastes effort; most slow training loops are bottlenecked somewhere unexpected.
concepts.body:
Before optimising, find the bottleneck. Common culprits are the data pipeline, CPU-GPU synchronisations and many small kernels, rather than the big matmuls.

**`torch.profiler.profile`** records operator-level CPU and CUDA activity:

- `activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]` chooses what to trace.
- `record_shapes=True` and `profile_memory=True` add shape and allocation information.
- Wrap regions with `record_function("data")` to label them in the trace.
- `prof.key_averages().table(sort_by=...)` prints the top operators; `prof.export_chrome_trace("trace.json")` writes a timeline you can open in Perfetto.

For training loops, pass `schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=1, warmup=1, active=3)` and call `prof.step()` each iteration, so you skip start-up noise and keep traces small.

What to look for in a timeline: gaps where the GPU is idle (data loading or Python overhead), many tiny kernels (candidates for `torch.compile`), and `cudaMemcpy` or synchronize calls in the middle of steps.

For micro-benchmarks, use **`torch.utils.benchmark.Timer`**. It handles warm-up and CUDA synchronisation and reports statistics, which naive `time.time()` measurements get wrong.
concepts.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.profiler import profile, record_function, ProfilerActivity
import torch.utils.benchmark as benchmark

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1024, 1024), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(1024, 10))
x = torch.randn(256, 1024)

activities = [ProfilerActivity.CPU]
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    activities.append(ProfilerActivity.CUDA)

with profile(activities=activities, record_shapes=True) as prof:
    with record_function("forward"):
        model(x)

print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cpu_time_total", row_limit=5))
prof.export_chrome_trace("trace.json")       # open in Perfetto

t = benchmark.Timer(stmt="model(x)", globals={"model": model, "x": x})
print(t.timeit(100))                         # mean time per run, warm-up handled
takeaways: Profile first: data loading and syncs are frequent bottlenecks
Label regions with `record_function`; view traces in Perfetto
Use `torch.utils.benchmark` for micro-benchmarks
pitfalls: Profiling the first iterations, which include warm-up, cuDNN autotuning and compilation.

quiz.q: A trace shows the GPU idle between steps while the CPU is busy in DataLoader code. What is the most likely fix?
quiz.explain: Idle GPU gaps filled by data work mean the input pipeline is the bottleneck.

concepts.name: DistributedDataParallel
concepts.summary: Train on several GPUs or machines with DDP: one process per GPU, launched by torchrun, with a DistributedSampler and gradient all-reduce.
concepts.why: DDP is the standard way to scale training beyond one GPU with near-linear speedup.
concepts.body:
**DistributedDataParallel (DDP)** runs one process per GPU. Each process holds a full model replica, trains on its own slice of every batch, and during `backward()` DDP **all-reduces** (averages) gradients across processes in buckets, overlapping communication with computation. After `step()` all replicas hold identical weights.

The moving parts:

- Launch with `torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py`. It starts the processes and sets `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK` and `WORLD_SIZE`.
- Each process calls `dist.init_process_group("nccl")` (use `"gloo"` on CPU), picks `cuda:LOCAL_RANK` and wraps the model: `DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank])`.
- A `DistributedSampler` gives each rank a disjoint shard of the data. Call `sampler.set_epoch(epoch)` each epoch, or every epoch uses the same shuffle.
- Save checkpoints, log and evaluate only on rank 0, and save `model.module.state_dict()`.

The **global batch** is per-GPU batch times world size; scale the learning rate accordingly or retune it. Use `nn.SyncBatchNorm.convert_sync_batchnorm(model)` if small per-GPU batches hurt BatchNorm.

Prefer DDP over the older `nn.DataParallel`, which is single-process and slower. When the model or optimizer state no longer fits on one GPU, move on to FSDP.
concepts.code:
# Launch: torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py
import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
from torch import nn
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler, TensorDataset
def main():
    dist.init_process_group("nccl")
    rank, local_rank = dist.get_rank(), int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)
    model = DDP(nn.Linear(10, 1).cuda(), device_ids=[local_rank])
    ds = TensorDataset(torch.randn(1024, 10), torch.randn(1024, 1))
    sampler = DistributedSampler(ds)                  # disjoint shard per rank
    loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, sampler=sampler)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    for epoch in range(3):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)                      # reshuffle each epoch
        for xb, yb in loader:
            loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(xb.cuda()), yb.cuda())
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()   # backward all-reduces
    if rank == 0:
        torch.save(model.module.state_dict(), "model.pt")
    dist.destroy_process_group()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
takeaways: One process per GPU, launched by torchrun
DistributedSampler + `set_epoch`; save and log on rank 0 only
Gradients are averaged during backward, so replicas stay in sync
pitfalls: Forgetting `sampler.set_epoch(epoch)`, so every epoch sees the same order.

quiz.q: With DDP on 8 GPUs and batch_size=32 in each DataLoader, what is the effective global batch size?
quiz.explain: Each of the 8 processes processes 32 samples per step and gradients are averaged over all of them.

concepts.name: Attention and transformer layers
concepts.summary: Use F.scaled_dot_product_attention for fast fused attention, understand the math behind it, and the built-in transformer layers.
concepts.why: Transformers dominate language, vision and audio; attention is their core and its kernel choice dominates speed and memory.
concepts.body:
**Attention** lets each position mix information from all others. For queries Q, keys K and values V of shape `(batch, heads, seq, head_dim)`:

`softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V`

A **causal** mask stops position i from attending to later positions, as needed for language-model decoding.

`torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None, is_causal=False, dropout_p=0.0)` computes exactly this but dispatches to fused kernels such as **FlashAttention** and memory-efficient attention when the inputs allow. These never materialise the full `seq x seq` score matrix, so memory grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically. Always prefer it over writing the softmax by hand.

To implement multi-head attention yourself, project the input with `nn.Linear` to Q, K, V, reshape `(B, T, H*D)` to `(B, H, T, D)`, call SDPA, then transpose back and project the output.

PyTorch also provides `nn.MultiheadAttention`, `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` and `nn.TransformerDecoderLayer` (pass `batch_first=True`; `norm_first=True` gives the pre-norm variant used by modern models). Most production LLM code writes its own blocks around SDPA, adding rotary position embeddings and KV caching.
concepts.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn

B, H, T, D = 2, 4, 16, 32                       # batch, heads, sequence, head dim
q, k, v = (torch.randn(B, H, T, D) for _ in range(3))

out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
print(out.shape)                                # torch.Size([2, 4, 16, 32])

# The same computation written out (materialises a T x T matrix):
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / D ** 0.5
causal = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
manual = scores.softmax(dim=-1) @ v
print(torch.allclose(out, manual, atol=1e-5))   # True

layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model=128, nhead=4, batch_first=True, norm_first=True)
print(layer(torch.randn(2, 16, 128)).shape)     # torch.Size([2, 16, 128])
takeaways: Attention = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V, per head
`scaled_dot_product_attention` picks fused Flash/efficient kernels
Heads live in a separate dim: (B, H, T, D)
pitfalls: Passing tensors as (B, T, H, D) to SDPA, which then treats T as the head dimension.

quiz.q: Why is FlashAttention-style SDPA more memory-efficient than the naive implementation?
options: It only attends to nearby tokens
It never materialises the full seq x seq attention matrix
quiz.explain: It computes attention in tiles with an online softmax, keeping memory linear in sequence length.

concepts.name: How autograd works
concepts.summary: The graph of grad_fn nodes, leaf tensors, saved tensors and version counters, and higher-order gradients with create_graph.
concepts.why: Understanding the engine explains in-place errors, memory use in backward, and how to compute Hessians or meta-gradients.
concepts.body:
During the forward pass, every differentiable op creates a **node** (`grad_fn`) holding references to the tensors it needs for its derivative (the **saved tensors**) and edges to the nodes of its inputs (`grad_fn.next_functions`). User-created tensors with `requires_grad=True` are **leaves**; they get an `AccumulateGrad` node that writes into `.grad`. Non-leaf tensors do not keep `.grad` unless you call `retain_grad()`.

`backward()` runs a topological traversal from the output, computing **vector-Jacobian products** node by node, so the cost of a full gradient is a small constant times the forward cost. Saved tensors are freed as soon as their node has run, which is why the default graph is single-use.

**In-place safety** comes from version counters. Every tensor has a `_version` that in-place ops increment.
